content: It is currently unclear whether dental care in individuals with periodontitis has any impact on their risk of developing cardiovascular disease. A diet rich in fruits and vegetables has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality. Evidence suggests that adherence to the Mediterranean diet may improve cardiovascular outcomes, including lowering cholesterol levels and blood pressure. The DASH diet, which emphasizes nuts, fish, fruits, and vegetables while limiting sweets, red meat, and fats, has been demonstrated to reduce blood pressure, lower total and LDL cholesterol, and improve metabolic syndrome. However, the long-term benefits of the DASH diet outside of clinical trial settings remain uncertain. A high-fiber diet appears to reduce cardiovascular risk, while total fat intake does not seem to be a significant risk factor. Diets high in trans fatty acids, however, are associated with increased rates of cardiovascular disease. Globally, dietary guidelines recommend reducing saturated fat intake, though the relationship between saturated fat and cardiovascular disease remains debated in the medical literature. Reviews from 2014 and 2015 did not find evidence of harm from saturated fats. A 2012 Cochrane review suggested a small benefit from replacing dietary saturated fats with unsaturated fats. However, a 2013 meta-analysis indicated that substituting saturated fats with omega-6 linoleic acid (a type of unsaturated fat) might increase cardiovascular risk. Replacing saturated fats with carbohydrates does not reduce risk and may even increase it. The greatest benefits appear to come from replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated fats, though supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids does not seem to have a significant effect. The impact of a low-salt diet is unclear. A Cochrane review concluded that any benefit in individuals with high or normal blood pressure is small, and a low-salt diet may even be harmful in those with congestive heart failure. However, this review was criticized for including a trial involving heart failure patients with low salt and water levels due to diuretics. Excluding this study, the remaining trials suggest a trend toward benefit. Another review found strong evidence that high dietary salt intake increases blood pressure, worsens hypertension, and raises the incidence of cardiovascular events, likely through mechanisms beyond just blood pressure elevation. Moderate evidence links high salt intake to increased cardiovascular mortality, and some evidence suggests associations with overall mortality, strokes, and left ventricular hypertrophy. Blood pressure-lowering medications reduce cardiovascular disease risk in at-risk individuals, regardless of age, baseline cardiovascular risk, or baseline blood pressure. Commonly used antihypertensive drug regimens are similarly effective in reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events, though specific drugs may differ in their ability to prevent certain outcomes. Greater reductions in blood pressure lead to greater reductions in risk, and most individuals with hypertension require multiple medications to achieve adequate blood pressure control. Statins are effective in preventing further cardiovascular events in individuals with a history of cardiovascular disease. Since event rates are higher in men than women, the reduction in events is more apparent in men. In individuals at risk but without a history of cardiovascular disease (primary prevention), statins reduce the risk of death and combined fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events. U.S. guidelines recommend statins for individuals with a 12% or greater 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease. Niacin, fibrates, and CETP inhibitors, while increasing HDL cholesterol, do not reduce cardiovascular disease risk in individuals already on statins. Anti-diabetic medications may reduce cardiovascular risk in individuals with type 2 diabetes, though evidence is inconclusive. Aspirin provides only modest benefit in individuals at low cardiovascular risk, as the risk of serious bleeding nearly offsets the cardiovascular benefit. It is not recommended for those at very low risk. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force advises against aspirin use for prevention in women under 55 and men under 45 but recommends it for some older individuals. The use of vasoactive agents in individuals with pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease or hypoxemic lung diseases may cause harm and unnecessary expense. Physical inactivity is estimated to account for 6% of the global burden of coronary heart disease. A systematic review estimated that 121,000 deaths from coronary heart disease in Europe in 2008 could have been prevented if physical inactivity had been eliminated. A Cochrane review found some evidence that yoga has favorable effects on blood pressure and cholesterol, though the included studies were of low quality. While a healthy diet is beneficial, antioxidant supplementation (e.g., vitamin E, vitamin C) and other vitamins have not been shown to protect against cardiovascular disease and may, in some cases, cause harm. Mineral supplements have also not been found to be useful. Niacin (vitamin B3) may modestly reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in high-risk individuals. Magnesium supplementation lowers high blood pressure in a dose-dependent manner and is recommended for individuals with ventricular arrhythmias associated with torsades de pointes and long QT syndrome, as well as for treating arrhythmias caused by digoxin toxicity. There is no evidence to support omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. Cardiovascular disease is treatable, with initial management focusing on dietary and lifestyle interventions. Influenza may increase the likelihood of heart attacks and strokes, and influenza vaccination may reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality in individuals with heart disease. Effective cardiovascular disease management requires prioritizing myocardial infarction and stroke cases due to their high combined mortality rates, while considering the cost-effectiveness of interventions, particularly in lowand middle-income countries.
